E6_mechanism: Pure dealership (specialist) market; unit trades; no limit orders.

E10.objective: The specialist sets bid and ask prices and earns zero expected profit on each purchase and each sale. There is no inventory objective and no utility function; competition among equally informed specialists is the stated mechanism producing the zero-profit condition.
E10.state_variables: Common-knowledge information S_t and trade history H_t; the specialist's conditional expectation E_t[V]; bid B_t and ask A_t, each a conditional expectation of V given the arriving order.
E10.payoff_support_assumed: Stated verbatim on p. 76: 'At some time T_0 in the future, some random dollar value V [V >= 0, var(V) < infinity] per share will be realized, and the informed have information about this random variable V.' No distributional form is imposed on V.
applicability_conditions_stated: Pure dealership market: 'the specialist performs no brokerage services, and in effect all orders are market orders' (p. 76).

Unit trades only, with the benefit stated: 'The assumption that only unit trades take place is restrictive, but it yields a corresponding benefit: It allows us to analyze a model that places no restrictions on the form of the traders' information.' Limit orders are ruled out, and the authors state that including them 'may well alter the characteristics of transaction prices'.
One arrival at any instant; the arrival process may otherwise depend on the history of trade.
The specialist earns zero expected profit on each trade, faces no transaction costs, and bears no cost on short positions in cash or stock.
The authors note that binding inventory constraints are inconsistent with the zero-profit condition and assume carrying capacity large enough that they do not bind.
E10.transfer_status_reason: The record states a payoff-support condition and a terminal realisation date: V >= 0 with finite variance, realised at T_0. That is precisely the kind of condition the transfer clause asks the corpus to state.
E10.corpus_inference_flag: A payoff bounded in [0,1] settling at an endpoint satisfies 'V >= 0, var(V) < infinity' and is realised at a terminal date. That satisfaction is THIS CORPUS'S inference from the authors' stated condition. The authors nowhere discuss binary, bounded or event contracts, and the corpus does not attribute such a discussion to them.
E10.authors_own_binary_example: Section 3, p. 91, verbatim: 'Suppose that the stock can have either of two values, V = 1 or V = 11, and that the higher value has prior probability pi.' The worked example is a two-point-valued security. The authors do not describe it as an event contract.

E15_kalshi_relevance: generalizable-with-stated-assumption. E6_mechanism: Limit order book; the agent posts one-share limit orders around the mid-price and is hit or lifted by incoming market orders.

E10.objective: Maximise the expected exponential (CARA) utility of the P&L profile at a terminal time T. The authors state the reason for the choice: it 'will allow us to define reservation (or indifference) prices which are independent of the agent's wealth'.
E10.state_variables: Mid-price S_t; inventory q; cash x; time to horizon T-t; quote distances delta^b and delta^a.
E10.payoff_support_assumed: Section 2.1: the mid-price evolves as dS_u = sigma dW_u with S_t = s, W a standard one-dimensional Brownian motion and sigma constant. Arithmetic Brownian motion on the real line; no boundary, no absorbing state, no bound. The authors' own footnote gives the reason for the choice: 'We choose this model over the standard geometric Brownian motion to ensure that the utility functionals introduced in the sequel remain bounded.'
applicability_conditions_stated: 'Underlying this continuous-time model is the implicit assumption that our agent has no opinion on the drift or any autocorrelation structure for the stock' (section 2.1).
'This mid-price will be used solely to value the agent's assets at the end of the investment period' - the terminal value is a mark-to-market at S_T, not a settlement at a contractual endpoint.

Market buy orders lift the agent's sell limit orders at Poisson rate lambda^a(delta^a), decreasing in delta^a, and symmetrically on the bid; 'For simplicity, we assume a constant frequency of market buy or sell orders.'
The money market pays no interest.
Limit orders are for one share, and the agent is committed to buy or sell one share if hit or lifted.
E10.transfer_status_reason: The model states its price process - driftless arithmetic Brownian motion with constant volatility, valued at T by mark-to-market.
E10.corpus_inference_flag: A driftless arithmetic Brownian motion is unbounded and has no absorbing endpoint, so it cannot be a probability confined to [0,1] that terminates at 0 or 1. That incompatibility is THIS CORPUS'S inference from the authors' stated dynamics; the authors nowhere discuss bounded-payoff or event contracts. This CORRECTS the 2026-09-02 entry, which recorded 'not addressed - the retrieved text states a securities-market setting and no bounded-payoff condition'. The full text does state a payoff-support condition; the earlier entry was an artefact of reading a publisher-truncated abstract.

E10.objective: The market maker maximises the expected CARA utility (coefficient gamma) of P&L over a finite horizon T, terminal value being cash X_T plus q_T S_T, the mark-to-market evaluation of the remaining signed inventory.

Crossref returns The Journal of Prediction Markets 1(1) 3-15 for the DOI (deposit date 2012-12-13). THE FILE IS THE AUTHOR'S JANUARY 2002 WORKING PAPER, NOT THE 2007 PUBLISHED ARTICLE. Title and author match and the text carries the Theorems 1 and 2 that the published abstract describes, but any wording difference between the 2002 manifestation and the 2007 publication is UNVERIFIED. Every quotation below is attributed to the 2002 manifestation and to nothing else.

E6_mechanism: Automated market maker / market scoring rule. There is no order book and no counterparty matching; the maker is the counterparty to every trade.

E10.objective: A market scoring rule market maker stands ready to pay any agent according to a proper scoring rule s_i(r) for changing the current report r; equivalently it is an automated market maker whose prices are the current report. The stated purpose is information aggregation, not profit.
E10.state_variables: Current report r over a complete set of I disjoint events; agents' asset holdings x_i; the logarithmic rule's parameter b.
E10.payoff_support_assumed: Assets are Arrow-Debreu claims. The paper's own description: an agent 'gains assets of the form "Pays $1 if A and B hold", in trade for assets of the form "Pays $1 if B holds and A does not"'. Per-unit payoffs are in {0,1} and the report r is a probability vector with sum_i r_i = 1.
applicability_conditions_stated: The events are a complete set of I disjoint events with sum_i p_i = 1.
The scoring rule must be PROPER: 'For a non-proper scoring rule, other reports also maximize an agent's expected payoff.'

'Expected monetary payoff will be maximized by risk-neutral agents with event-independent utility. Other agents can also be induced to maximize an expected monetary payoff' - the footnote gives the lottery-ticket device as the means.
Theorem 1: 'Logarithmic rule bets on A given B preserve p(B), and for any event C preserve p(C|AB), p(C|~AB), and p(C|~B), and thus preserve I(A,B,C), and I(B,A,C).'

Theorem 2, the uniqueness half: 'For I >= 3, if y_i = 0 for i not in {j,k} implies q_i = 0 for i not in {j,k}, the rule is logarithmic.' The locality that motivates modular combinatorial use holds ONLY for the logarithmic version and only for at least three events.

COST CONDITION the author states against his own mechanism: for the logarithmic rule the maximum expected cost of a full combinatorial report is no more than the cost of base-only reports 'at least when the parameter b is held constant', but 'it remains difficult to bound the computational cost of updating prices and assets', which 'can be large, being worse than polynomial in the worst case'.
E10.transfer_status_reason: The bounded payoff is the premise, not an assumption to be relaxed: the traded assets are $1-if-event claims and the market state is a probability vector.
E10.authors_own_binary_example: The whole construction is over $1-if-event assets.

E6_mechanism: Automated market maker in the thick-market case; simple scoring rule in the thin-market case.

E10.objective: Design an information market that aggregates information over a joint probability distribution on many variables. Market scoring rules act as an automated market maker in the thick-market case and as a simple scoring rule in the thin-market case; the stated design goal is to avoid the thin-market and irrational-participation problems of standard markets and the opinion-pooling problem of scoring rules.
E10.state_variables: A joint probability distribution over combinations of base variable values; user asset positions; the scoring-rule parameter.
E10.payoff_support_assumed: Bets on variable-value combinations; the design problem is stated over a joint probability distribution, so state prices lie in the simplex and per-unit payoffs are $1-if-combination.
applicability_conditions_stated: 'Logarithmic versions have cost and modularity advantages' - the advantage is stated for the logarithmic version specifically, not for market scoring rules in general.

Three design conditions the author states the mechanism must satisfy to work in practice: how to represent variables so as to support both conditional and unconditional estimates; how to avoid becoming a money pump via errors in calculating probabilities; and how to ensure that users can cover their bets, without needlessly preventing them from using previous bets as collateral for future bets.

The third is a COLLATERAL condition, and it is the author's own statement that the mechanism's viability depends on a settlement and collateral rule and not on the pricing rule alone. It is the only statement in the S4 native literature this corpus read at full text that reaches strand S5.
E10.transfer_status_reason: Payoffs are $1-if-combination claims over a joint outcome space; boundedness is the premise.
E10.authors_own_binary_example: Bets on combinations of base variable values.

E15_kalshi_relevance: generalizable-with-stated-assumption; carrying assumption as for Hanson (2007).
